lines: Kill off one worker on purpose, right in the middle of everything, and time how long it takes to come back.
That time has nothing to do with how many steps the whole job happens to be made of.
It tracks one thing only: how much was actually sitting on that one worker when it went down.
A picture gets taken of everything, consistently, while the whole thing keeps on running underneath.
What that picture actually contains, piece by piece, for work that's organized around a key, is the open question here.
Answering that is also what makes resizing the whole thing afterward even possible at all.
Worth reasoning through before the reveal settles it.
The whole thing gets resized, bigger or smaller, and whatever was being kept has to go somewhere.
Does each individual piece get relocated on its own, one at a time, or does something else happen instead?
answer: Something else happens. Fixed groups move together, as whole blocks.
Every single piece was already sorted into one of a fixed number of groups, decided from the very start.
Resizing moves those groups around whole. It never reaches in and relocates one piece by itself.

lines: Every single piece gets sorted into exactly one of a fixed number of groups, and that sorting never changes.
That number of groups gets decided once, way up front, completely separate from how many workers happen to exist right now.
From that point on, it's the groups that get handed out to workers, never the individual pieces.
Resize the whole thing, and entire groups slide over to different workers, all at once, as one unit.
No group ever gets torn in half across two different workers. That split simply doesn't happen.
Check every single piece afterward, and it comes back exactly as it was, nothing lost or changed.
One way of keeping things close by is plain and fast, but only holds as much as memory allows.
A different way trades some of that speed away, in exchange for far more room, out on disk instead.
Pick one over the other, and that's the trade being made: quick and limited, or roomier and slower.
Worth reasoning through once more before this reveal settles it.
One version of the job is simple. A very different version does a whole lot more, step after step.
Does that heavier, more involved version take noticeably longer to come back after the exact same kind of failure?
answer: No. What each version is doing makes no difference at all to that.
Coming back only depends on how much was sitting on the worker that went down, nothing about the job's shape.
Run both, lose the same worker both times, and they come back in exactly the same amount of time.

lines: Run it for real, side by side, one simple and one far more elaborate, losing the identical worker.
They come back in the same amount of time, every single time, with no exception at all.
Only a worker holding noticeably more actually takes noticeably longer. Nothing else about the job matters here.
Leave something sitting untouched for long enough, and it quietly expires and gets cleared away on its own.
Nobody has to go reach in and remove it by hand. That cleanup just happens, on a best effort basis.
A shape can also change a little over time, but only within a narrow, clearly spelled out set of allowed moves.
A much bigger jump, from an older version of everything to a genuinely newer one, is a separate question.

The coming-back time that really didn't care how elaborate either version of the job happened to be.

Resizing slides those whole groups around, never tears one apart, and whatever's inside checks out clean.
